transcript:
[00:00] Lena Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro - I m Lena from Redwood, AE. Marco our SE will cover reliability patterns.
[00:12] Priya Sharma: Hey, Priya here. Thanks, we re evaluating options — hosted vs dedicated vs private — mostly around reliability and incident tolerance.
[00:20] Marco Diaz: Great, Priya. Quick agenda: understand your stack, failure modes, success criteria and then walk through multi-region and fallback patterns.
[00:28] Tom Nguyen: Cool. To start, we re an e-commerce platform, heavy traffic US + EU; peak events, Black Friday-ish. We need p95 <= 300ms for checkout inference and system must not fail open.
[00:40] Marco Diaz: Understood. For p95 targets, are those end-to-end or just model inference?
[00:46] Tom Nguyen: Model only. End-to-end is 500ms but inference is critical.
[00:51] Alicia Gomez: From security side, we need audit logs, KMS support, and SOC2. Also data residency — EU must stay in EU for EU customers.
[01:02] Lena Park: Makes sense. Quick Q: are you currently self-hosting models or using a third-party API?
[01:07] Priya Sharma: We use a mix — some in house for embeddings, some API for chat. We re exploring Redwood because of the dedicated pools and private deploy info.
[01:15] Speaker 1: (mumble) how do you do fallbacks — like if a model times out?
[01:19] Marco Diaz: Good question. Redwood supports layered fallback policies: route to a lower-cost/compatible variant, or to a cached response, or to a different region. You can configure ordered policies and timeouts.
[01:31] Tom Nguyen: How does multi-region routing work? We d prefer active-active with region preference and automatic failover.
[01:39] Marco Diaz: We have smart routing — you can set policies by latency, cost, or region. For active-active, we do request-level routing with health checks and can fail traffic to the other region if a pool is degraded. We also support sticky sessions for KV cache locality to avoid cold KV cache hits.
[01:53] Priya Sharma: Sticky sessions — do you mean the KV cache is region-specific?
[01:57] Marco Diaz: Yes, the KV cache is per serving pool. If you route across region, you ll either rehydrate or use prefix caching. We also support prefix/KV caching across regions with replication, but there s added cost and eventual consistency.
[02:10] Alicia Gomez: What about SLA? We need something we can hold the vendor to.
[02:15] Lena Park: For Dedicated we offer SLA-backed latency and uptime targets — typically 99.9% uptime with latency SLOs per route. Hosted has best-effort with published performance profiles; we can discuss enterprise SLA add-ons.
[02:27] Tom Nguyen: Can you give an example of how you handle incidents? Say a version of a model starts returning huge latencies or errors.
[02:34] Marco Diaz: Typically we have canary deploys + automatic rollback. In the runtime, if error rates or p95 cross thresholds, routing can shift to a fallback model or to a previous pinned version. For hosted customers we also have region-level fallbacks and degraded-mode policies — e.g., switch to a cheaper small model to preserve availability.
[02:52] Priya Sharma: So you re saying we could configure a policy: if p95 > 400ms for 2 minutes, route 30% traffic to fallback, then 100% if 5 minutes?
[03:01] Marco Diaz: Exactly. You can do gradual canary fallbacks, A/B and progressive ramp-downs.
[03:06] Tom Nguyen: And how fast is the failover between regions? If EU loses its pool, how many seconds to route to US?
[03:12] Marco Diaz: Health checks are sub-10s by default; plus we have a routing cooldowns to avoid flapping. In practice region failovers often happen within 10-30s depending on DNS and your client TTLs. For low-latency clients we suggest our edge routing or persistent connections which cut that down.
[03:28] Priya Sharma: About VPC/private — if we do Private (VPC or on-prem), how are fallbacks handled? We d want private-first but fallback to Redwood Hosted only if allowed.
[03:39] Marco Diaz: For Private deployments we support cross-tier routing: you can define primary on your Private control plane, and Redwood Hosted as secondary. We do encrypted tunnels and egress rules. There s also an option to keep metadata and logs in your control plane for audit.
[03:52] Alicia Gomez: Encryption at rest/in transit — we need HSM/KMS integration and key control.
[03:56] Lena Park: We integrate with customer KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, HSM) for Dedicated and Private; Hosted can use Redwood-managed keys by default or customer-managed keys via BYOK for enterprise.
[04:10] Tom Nguyen: If we failover to hosted regionally, what happens to data residency constraints?
[04:16] Marco Diaz: Good catch. If you re under EU data residency, we d recommend only routing EU traffic to EU-hosted pools. Fallback to non-EU requires legal signoff and specific contract clauses. We can also do anonymization or partial responses as an interim.
[04:30] Priya Sharma: Observability — we need per-request traces and token-level latency. How accessible is that?
[04:36] Marco Diaz: Redwood Console exposes token-level cost/latency, per-route dashboards, traces and request logs. For Dedicated/Private we can stream logs to your SIEM. There s also instrumentation hooks for distributed tracing.
[04:49] Alicia Gomez: Audit logs retention — can we set retention and export?
[04:53] Lena Park: Yes, retention is configurable for Dedicated and Private; Hosted has tiers. Exports to S3 or to your chosen storage are supported.
[05:00] Tom Nguyen: Okay pricing comment — dedicated pools are attractive but cost is a concern. How to balance latency vs cost?
[05:06] Marco Diaz: We usually recommend a hybrid: keep mission-critical routes on Dedicated with strict SLOs, and route lower priority traffic to hosted or lower-capacity variants. Batching and KV cache wins also reduce tokens and latency. Redwood Optimize gives quantization and batching suggestions per workload.
[05:21] Priya Sharma: Do you support model quantization on Dedicated?
[05:24] Marco Diaz: Yes — we support standard quantization profiles and can recommend based on your accuracy/latency targets. There s runtime support for int8 paths on supported GPUs.
[05:33] Speaker 2: (brief crosstalk) and what about peak bursting?
[05:37] Marco Diaz: Dedicated has autoscaling and burst policies; you can pre-warm and reserve buffer capacity. For extreme peaks we can fold in Hosted for overflow.
[05:44] Priya Sharma: Can we pin model versions for compliance?
[05:47] Lena Park: Absolutely. Version pinning + rollouts with canary are standard.
[05:51] Tom Nguyen: On failure modes, do you preserve request queueing or do you reject? We need to avoid silent failures.
[05:58] Marco Diaz: You can configure degraded-mode behavior: queue with retries, return cached response, degrade to shorter outputs, or reject with explicit errors. We log all decisions so you have observability into failures.
[06:11] Alicia Gomez: A practical ask — can you send security docs and a sample SLA?
[06:15] Lena Park: Yes, I ll send SOC2, pen-test summary, our standard SLA and a template for data residency clauses.
[06:22] Marco Diaz: I ll also draft a benchmark plan that covers multi-region failover tests, p95 targets, and fallback correctness.
[06:28] Priya Sharma: Great. Let s plan a POC around our next traffic spike window.
[06:33] Lena Park: Sounds good. Quick recap — we ll send security docs, Marco will share benchmark plan and pricing for Dedicated, Tom will share traffic profiles, and we ll set a follow-up for Oct 6 to discuss SSO and network.
[06:47] Tom Nguyen: Thanks, everyone. Appreciate the concrete patterns.
[06:50] Lena Park: Thanks all — we ll follow up with notes and the docs.
[06:55] (call ends)
